authoring.value:
We proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}3\cdot {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{3\cdot {4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[3\cdot {4}^{x}]}_{a}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(3-3\cdot {4}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\cdot (3-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }3\cdot {4}^{a})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y={4}^{x}$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }{4}^{x}=0$

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{4}^{x}=\infty $

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056962/assets/fd4020291b348d130fc34969d72ff683aab5b6fb95ea5f7d32b90e5245d56d9c.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}3\cdot {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\cdot (3-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }3\cdot {4}^{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}\cdot (3-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(4)}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we substitute $u=\sqrt{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,⟹\,2\text{d}u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=\sqrt{x}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{6}^{-2u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{{6}^{-2u}}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡6}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{6}^{-2u}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14056962/assets/8f732515dd376db40889706419781e02cbedfcd4da8513a09e4f2d77ff88ece2.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{6}^{-2\sqrt{x}}}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{6}^{2a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}.\end{aligned}
$$
